Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters View image in fullscreen The US, Europe and Saudi Arabia are reportedly putting pressure on Oman to accept an arrangement on reopening the strait of Hormuz with a temporary shipping route. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters Iran US and Qatar report progress on Iran ceasefire and reopening Hormuz strait Optimism echoes Trump’s claims on Monday that deal is close as mediators say they are exchanging proposals Middle East crisis live – latest updates Julian Borger and Patrick Wintour Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.19 EDT First published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US and Qatari officials have said progress is being made in restoring a ceasefire in the US-Iran war and reopening the strait of Hormuz. The optimistic speculation on Tuesday brought oil prices down 2%, but the strait remained closed to shipping and a cargo vessel was reportedly struck by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast close to the strait. Britain’s maritime security agency, UKMTO, reported the strike on Monday night but did not name the vessel. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said the US and Iran were negotiating and told CNBC television: “I think there is a chance we may have a deal today ​or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised ​position in this conflict.” His remarks echo similarly upbeat comments on Monday from Donald Trump , who claimed that a breakthrough was imminent, though Tehran quickly denied it was involved in any direct talks with the US. Qatari and Pakistani mediators said they were talking to both sides in an effort to close gaps, restore the ceasefire deal from the memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed in mid-June and reopen the Hormuz strait, which was the portal for a fifth of the world’s oil and liquified natural gas. Qatar’s ‌foreign ministry spokesperson, Majed al-Ansari, said Qatar, Pakistan and Oman were mediating in close coordination and exchanging draft proposals between Washington and Tehran. He said the diplomatic contacts had reached “very progressive stages”. A senior Pakistani security official told Reuters news agency: “A lot is happening in the ‌background … We are talking to both sides. Our sole goal at this moment is to make both parties at least agree to start talking.” However, neither Qatar nor Pakistan are directly involved in the focus of negotiations in recent days, which has been between Iran and Oman on a temporary transit scheme that would allow ships to enter and leave the Gulf. The MoU broke down in July when vessels tried to cross the strait along the Omani coast without seeking Iranian approval, and Iran attacked them. Regional diplomats involved in the talks said Oman was under concerted US, European and Saudi pressure to accept a temporary scheme that would allow shipping to enter the Gulf via a route through the strait close to Iran, and then leave on a southern route along the Omani coast, which would be jointly controlled with Iran. The contentious issue of Iran’s demand to charge transiting vessels tolls or other fees would be left to be decided during a 60-day negotiating period, during which time Iran’s nuclear programme would also be addressed. The Omani government has been resisting the Hormuz proposal out of fear it could become permanent and give Tehran an enduring say over sea routes in Omani waters, the regional diplomats said. The Iranian state-run broadcaster IRIB reported on Tuesday evening: “These negotiations, taking place between the two coastal countries of the strait of Hormuz, are focused on determining safe routes for ships to transit. The talks have so far been assessed as positive at both the technical and political levels, and Iran is working with Oman to develop the necessary mechanisms for future arrangements to manage shipping traffic in this strategic waterway.” The talks are complicated by splits in Tehran, according to the diplomats, with the foreign ministry keen to do a deal and fearing Iranian control of the Hormuz strait could prove to be a wasting asset over time as sea traffic finds alternative routes. Regime hardliners, on the other hand, oppose the deal on the grounds that the US administration cannot be trusted to deliver the financial benefits promised in return for opening the strait. “I think the regime understands the magnitude of the hold Iran has over the strait, and they smell the desperation coming from the US in terms of [trying to] strike a deal,” a diplomat from the region said. Another diplomat said Riyadh was putting particularly heavy pressure on Oman because the Saudis thought “we may be on the brink of a regional war because there is a big faction in Iran that does not want a deal under any circumstances”. https://www.politico.eu/article/former-b.text: LONDON — Architects of the U.K.’s post-Brexit “red lines” now back a rethink on the EU relations strictures at the next election. Nick Thomas-Symonds, who served as former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s top negotiator with Brussels, said that Britain should be open to getting rid of the boundaries in the interest of economic growth. The former Cabinet minister, who led “reset” talks with the EU until July, was one of the staunchest defenders of the red lines — which rule out rejoining the single market, the customs union and restoring freedom of movement. Advertisement Advertisement Labour campaigned and won the 2024 general election on those promises as it sought to move the Brexit conversation on after years of fractious debate. Thomas-Symonds is the latest Starmer ally to express openness to dropping those restrictions in Labour's manifesto at the next election (which must be held before the end of summer 2029). The comments further demonstrate the shift in opinion in the Labour Party, and its belief that public sentiment has moved with it. Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet with continental leaders at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin Thursday to help progress another incremental “reset” deal with Brussels that should be signed at a EU-U.K. summit in Brussels. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged to put Britain on a "new path" by rejecting 40 years of privatisation, austerity, and Brexit on the final day of the Labour Party conference at Liverpool Experience Campus on Sept. 30, 2026. | Ian Forsyth/Getty Images Around that Nov. 20 summit, the prime minister has committed to go further in setting out what he thinks the options are for future relations with the bloc. He hasn’t taken the option of Britain fully rejoining the EU off the table. “We do need to have a debate now about what we want to do going forward,” Thomas-Symonds said in an interview in his office in parliament on Tuesday. The MP for Torfaen said that during his time as a Cabinet Office minister he had frequent conversations with British and European businesses about the post-Brexit red tape holding them back. Advertisement Advertisement “Now that is not helping us in terms of growing the economy. So the kind of growth potential is significant,” he added. “So, given the status quo is not working in the way that it should be, given I think where public opinion is as well, I don't think anyone was interested in another Brexit election in 2024 — but certainly now where public opinion is as well, I think it's absolutely right to have a debate now about these different options that are available to us.” Thomas-Symonds’ comments come after Chris Ward — a former Cabinet Office minister and long-time political aide to Starmer who helped draw up the red lines — said those red lines deserve a “ dignified retirement .” Rachel Reeves, who was Starmer's chief finance minister, said this month that Britain should go back into the EU — comments which would have been impossible to voice while serving in his administration. Veteran Brexiteer Nigel Farage has called Burnham’s approach a “total betrayal” and hopes it could reinvigorate his Reform UK party — which has been on a downward trajectory in the polls. “I think I probably know the pitfalls of it more than most,” said Thomas-Symonds of escalating the Brexit conversation. “But this is a necessary debate to have because we do need to reach a position to put the future relationship with the European Union on a firm footing.” But he called for an “open debate” and for the costs and benefits of the various options for a closer relationship with the EU to be transparently laid out. Britain could continue to try to broker bespoke arrangements, rejoin the customs union, single market, or the bloc itself. Advertisement Advertisement “What we need to see is all these things set out with the trade-offs because we can't just have a debate in the abstract again,” said Thomas-Symonds, who returned to the backbenches after Burnham took over from Starmer. Burnham appointed Hamish Falconer as his minister for EU relations. Burnham's decision to trigger the EU debate is facing skepticism in his own Cabinet, where some ministers are sensitive to reopening the old wounds of the Brexit debate. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood have both historically been hesitant about re-litigating Brexit battles. Chancellor John Healey put a dampener on Burnham’s grander hopes that Britain will rejoin the EU in his lifetime, telling Channel 4 News last month that he does not expect that to happen.
